transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well… I suppose what brings me in is that once I start worrying, I can’t seem to turn it off. I’ll tell myself, “All right, you’ve made the list, you checked the dates, you’ve done what you reasonably can do,” but my mind just keeps going back over it anyway.

It’s not that I’m trying to be dramatic about it. I know everyone worries, and at my age there are always things to keep track of, but this feels like my brain doesn’t accept that something is settled. I can do the practical steps, and even after that, I’m still sitting there turning it over and over. That’s really why I thought I should come in and talk to someone.
Do you experience any physical symptoms like tension, headaches, or stomach issues when you're worrying?

Yes, mostly tension. I notice it especially by the end of the day, like I’ve been holding myself stiff without realizing it. My shoulders and neck get so tight, and then I’ll catch myself clenching my jaw when I’m just sitting and reading or going over plans for the garden center activities.

It’s funny, because in the moment I don’t always think, “Oh, I’m tense.” I’m just trying to get through the list in my head or make sure I haven’t missed something. But later I realize I’ve been braced all day, like my body was preparing for something even though I was just at home or doing ordinary things.
Do you find yourself avoiding certain activities or situations because of your worries?

Yes… not avoiding completely, I suppose, because I still do go. I’m still keeping up with the garden activities and the book club, and I don’t want to give the impression that I’ve stopped my life or anything like that. But I have noticed I’m pulling back around the edges.

For example, with the garden center exhibitions, I used to take on more of the planning without thinking much of it—checking details, helping organize things, that sort of thing. Lately, I’ve been turning down pieces of it, or saying someone else might be better suited, because it feels like too much to manage. And even when I do show up, I’m sometimes less prepared than I used to be, which bothers me because I’ve always been fairly dependable.

So it’s not that I won’t leave the house or won’t see people. It’s more that I’m choosing the smaller, safer role, if that makes sense, because the bigger planning parts set off too much worrying.
Have you noticed any changes in your mood or interest in activities you normally enjoy?

I’m not sure I’d say my mood has changed in a clear way. I mean, I have moments where I feel worn down by all the worrying, but I wouldn’t say I’ve lost interest in the things I usually enjoy.

I still like going to the garden center, and I still like the book club. Sometimes I arrive feeling a bit preoccupied, or I don’t throw myself into things quite as easily because my mind is elsewhere, but once I’m there, I can usually enjoy parts of it. So… no, I don’t think it’s that I’ve stopped caring about those things. It’s more that the worry sort of sits on top of them, if that makes sense.
Do you have thoughts that repeat over and over in your mind, even when you try to stop thinking about them?

Yes, very much so. That’s actually what brings me in, more than anything else, I think. Once the worrying starts, I can’t seem to turn it off, even when I know, logically, that I’ve already done what I can.

I’ll tell myself, “You’ve made the list, you’ve checked the dates, you’ve written it down, there’s nothing else to do right now,” but my mind doesn’t seem to accept that. It just keeps circling back, like maybe I missed something or should go over it one more time. And then if I try to distract myself, it might quiet down for a few minutes, but it comes right back in. It’s not always one dramatic thought, it’s more this repeated reviewing and checking in my mind, over and over.

I know it probably sounds like ordinary planning, and I’ve always been someone who likes to be prepared, but this feels different because it doesn’t stop when the practical part is finished. That’s the frustrating bit. I can see that I’ve done all I reasonably can, but I still can’t get my mind to let it go.
Is your worrying usually about one specific thing or are you worrying about a wide range of things?

It’s definitely not just one thing. I almost wish it were, because then I could say, “Right, this is the problem,” and deal with that. But it sort of moves around.

One minute I’m thinking about the exhibition schedule at the garden center—whether I’ve remembered the right dates, whether someone else has the information they need, whether I’ve overlooked some small detail. Then before I’ve even finished with that thought, my mind jumps to my daughter’s travel plans, and I’m wondering if everything will go smoothly for her, or if there’s something she hasn’t thought of. And then it’ll be something completely ordinary, like whether the gutters on the house need fixing, and suddenly that feels as if it could turn into a much bigger problem if I don’t deal with it soon enough.

So, no, it isn’t one specific worry. It’s more like my mind keeps roaming from one concern to the next, and small things start to feel as if they could unravel into something much larger.
Have you ever experienced a sudden, intense feeling of fear or discomfort that reached a peak within minutes?

I don’t think so, not in that sudden way you’re describing. I mean, I do get very uncomfortable when I’m worrying, and sometimes it can feel quite intense, but it’s more like it builds and lingers rather than coming on all at once and peaking within a few minutes.

I wouldn’t say I’ve had an episode where fear just suddenly hits me out of nowhere and then reaches a peak quickly. It’s more that my mind gets caught on something, and the tension sort of grows from there. So… no, I don’t think I’ve experienced that, at least not as I understand what you mean.
Do you often feel restless or on edge when you're worrying?

Yes, I do. It’s not always dramatic, but I often feel sort of wound up, even when I’m just sitting at home in my own living room. I’ll be sitting there and I can feel this jumpiness in me, like I can’t quite settle.

If I’m on the phone, especially if it’s about something I’ve been worrying over, I notice I’ll tap my fingers without really meaning to. Or I’ll get up and straighten a cushion, or move something on the table, or check that something is put away properly—not because it desperately needs doing, but because sitting still feels uncomfortable. It’s as if my body is looking for something to do while my mind is going over everything.

Sometimes I’ll think, “Why can’t you just sit quietly for five minutes?” But I feel too on edge, too keyed up. Even in a perfectly calm room, I don’t always feel calm inside.
Has your worrying affected your relationships with family or friends in any way?

A little, yes. I wouldn’t say it’s caused some big falling-out or anything like that, but it has started to affect how I show up for people and for the things I normally do.

I still go to the garden club and the book club, and I do enjoy them once I’m there, mostly. But I’ve noticed I’m not quite as prepared as I used to be. With the book club, I might have read the book but not really gathered my thoughts properly, or I’ll arrive feeling as if I’ve forgotten something. And with the garden center exhibition planning, I’ve started saying no to bits of it that I probably would have taken on before. Not because I don’t care—if anything, I care too much and then it all feels harder to manage.

I think people probably just see it as me scaling back a little, but inside it feels more like I’m avoiding the parts that might overwhelm me. I don’t want to let anyone down, so I still keep involved, but I’m not as dependable or as on top of things as I used to be, and that bothers me.
Do you feel like your worrying is interfering with your daily life or overall well-being?

Yes, I think it is, though maybe not in a dramatic way. I’m still doing the things I usually do — I still go to the garden club and the book club, and I don’t want to make it sound like I’ve completely withdrawn or stopped functioning. I haven’t.

But it’s definitely changed the way I manage those things. I’ve noticed I’m arriving less prepared than I used to. With the book club, for example, I might still have read what I’m meant to read, but I don’t feel as organized in my thoughts, or I haven’t made the notes I normally would. And with the garden club, especially the exhibition planning, I’ve started turning down parts of it that I probably would have agreed to before.

It’s not that I don’t care about it — I do. That’s part of what bothers me. It just feels harder to manage than it used to, and I find myself backing away from the bits that feel like they might become too much. So yes, I’d say it’s interfering with my daily life and my general sense of being on top of things, even if I’m still keeping up appearances to some extent.
Do you avoid certain situations because you fear they will trigger intense anxiety or worry?

Yes, I suppose I do, though maybe I wouldn’t have called it “avoidance” at first. I’m not avoiding everything — I still go to the garden club and the book club, and I do want to keep those things in my life. They matter to me, and once I’m there, I usually manage.

But I’ve noticed I’m sort of quietly stepping back from the parts that feel as though they might become too much. With the book club, I’ll still turn up, but I’m less prepared than I used to be — not as organized, not having thought things through properly beforehand. And with the garden exhibition planning, I’ve started turning down little jobs or pieces of it that I probably would have said yes to before.

It’s not that I’m afraid of the garden club itself, exactly. It’s more that if something feels like it might set off a lot of worry or make me feel overloaded, I find myself saying, “Oh, maybe someone else should do that,” or “I’m not sure I can take that on.” So yes, in that sense, I think I am avoiding certain situations, or at least avoiding the more demanding parts, because they feel harder to manage than they used to.
Do you ever feel compelled to perform specific rituals or routines to reduce your worrying?

No, I don’t think so. At least, not in the sense of having a particular ritual I feel I have to do, like checking something a certain number of times or repeating a routine to make the worry go away.

I do have habits, I suppose — I might look over my calendar more than once, or think through what I’m meant to be doing the next day, but that feels more like trying to reassure myself or get organized than a set ritual. I don’t feel like, “If I don’t do this exact thing, something terrible will happen.” It’s more just that my mind keeps circling around things, and I’ll try to settle it by going over them again.

So no, I haven’t noticed any specific ritual or routine like that. It’s more the worrying itself than anything I’m compelled to do because of it.
Do you feel like you're able to control your worrying most of the time?

Not really, no. I mean, I can sometimes distract myself for a bit, or I can tell myself very firmly, “You’ve already made the list, you’ve checked the dates, you’ve done what you can,” but it doesn’t seem to switch off just because I’ve said that.

That’s really part of what brings me in, I suppose. Once the worry gets going, it sort of keeps running in the background, even when there isn’t anything more for me to do about it. I’ll know, logically, that I’ve handled the practical side of things, but my mind keeps going back over it anyway — did I miss something, should I check again, what if I’ve forgotten some small detail.

So I wouldn’t say I’m able to control it most of the time. I can sometimes contain it, maybe, or keep functioning around it, but I don’t feel like I can reliably make it stop when I want to.
Do you often feel like you're fidgeting or have an inability to relax when you're not worrying about something specific?

Yes… I think so. Even when I’m not worrying about one particular thing, I often feel sort of wound up, like my body hasn’t got the message that there’s nothing urgent happening.

It happens at home quite a bit, which feels silly to say because I’m just in my own living room, where I should be comfortable. I’ll be sitting there and find myself tapping my fingers on the arm of the chair, or shifting around, or feeling like I need to get up and do something. If I’m on the phone, I notice my fingers tapping or I’ll start fussing with something nearby. And sometimes I’ll get up to straighten a cushion or move a pile of papers, not because it really needs doing, but because sitting still feels oddly uncomfortable.

It’s not dramatic, exactly. I’m not pacing around all day. But quiet sitting doesn’t feel as restful as it used to. There’s this jumpy feeling, like I’m waiting for something, even if I couldn’t tell you what.
Do you have thoughts that are intrusive or unwanted, and that you try to suppress or ignore?

I’m not sure I’d describe it that way, no. I mean, I do have thoughts I don’t particularly want — worries that pop up when I’d rather be thinking about something else — but they usually feel like ordinary worries that have got stuck on repeat, not like strange or shocking thoughts that come out of nowhere.

When you say “intrusive,” I think of something that feels very alien or disturbing, and I don’t really have that. It’s more that I’ll find myself thinking, “What if I’ve overlooked something?” or “What if this turns out badly?” and then I try not to dwell on it, but trying not to think about it doesn’t always work. It’s not so much that I’m suppressing some awful image or idea; it’s more like I’m trying to put the worry aside and my mind keeps picking it back up.

So… no, not in the way I think you mean. I have unwanted worries, certainly, but I wouldn’t say I have intrusive thoughts that I’m trying to suppress or ignore in a more specific sense.
Do you often worry about everyday things, like finances, health, or relationships, even when there's no apparent reason to worry?

Yes, I do. More than I think is reasonable, honestly. It isn’t always one big obvious problem — it’s more that my mind sort of wanders from one ordinary thing to the next and treats each one as if it might become serious if I don’t keep thinking about it.

For example, I’ll start thinking about the exhibition schedule — whether I’ve remembered the dates properly, whether something might clash, whether I’ve misunderstood some small arrangement — and then before I’ve even settled that, my mind has moved on to my daughter’s travel plans. I’ll wonder if she’s left enough time, if the trains or flights will be all right, whether I should check in with her, even when there’s no real reason to think anything is wrong.

And then it can shift again to the house, like the gutters. I’ll notice a bit of rain or remember they haven’t been looked at in a while, and suddenly it feels as though if I don’t think it through properly, it could turn into some much bigger problem — water damage, repairs, expense, all of that. I know that sounds like making a mountain out of a molehill, and part of me does know that, but in the moment these small everyday things start to feel as if they could unravel. So yes, even without an obvious reason, I do find myself worrying about ordinary things quite a lot.
Do you feel like your worrying is significantly affecting your overall quality of life?

Yes… I think it is, though I suppose I’d say it’s not ruining my life or anything like that. I still do the things that matter to me. I’m still out in the garden, and I still go to book club, and from the outside I probably look as if I’m managing perfectly well.

But it has started to affect how well I do things, if that makes sense. With book club, for instance, I still go, but I’m not always as prepared as I used to be. I’ll mean to finish the reading properly or make a few notes, and then I find I’ve spent all this time going over other things in my head, or feeling too unsettled to sit down and concentrate on it. So I arrive and feel a bit embarrassed, because I used to be more on top of it.

And with the exhibition planning, that’s probably where I notice it more. I haven’t stopped completely, but I’ve started stepping back from parts of it. If there’s something that involves coordinating details or being responsible for too many moving pieces, I’m more likely now to say, “Oh, perhaps someone else should take that,” or I’ll avoid volunteering. It just feels harder to manage than it used to, even if the actual task isn’t impossible.

So yes, my quality of life is still there, but it feels a bit narrowed, I suppose. I’m still participating, but not with the same ease or confidence.
Do you feel like your worrying is making it hard for you to enjoy the things you used to?

Yes, I think so… not completely, but enough that I notice it. I still do the things I’ve always enjoyed — I’m still in the garden, and I still go to book club, so it’s not as if I’ve withdrawn altogether. But they don’t feel quite as easy or absorbing as they used to.

With the garden, I can still get out there and potter about, and sometimes it does help, actually. But there are times when I’m out there and instead of just enjoying the plants or noticing what needs pruning, my mind is half somewhere else, going over other responsibilities or little things I think I may have missed. So I’m doing it, but not always getting the same pleasure from it.

Book club is similar. I still go, and I’m glad I do, but I’ve started turning up less prepared than I’d like. I used to be someone who had read the book properly and had thoughts about it, and now sometimes I’ve only half-read it or I haven’t taken it in properly because my mind’s been busy with other worries. Then I sit there feeling a bit self-conscious, which takes some of the enjoyment out of it.

And with the exhibition planning, I’ve definitely started stepping back from bits I might have taken on before. If something feels like it has too many details or too much responsibility, I’m more likely to turn it down or let someone else handle it. It’s frustrating, because I do enjoy being involved, but it feels harder to manage than it used to. So yes — I still do these things, but the worry sort of dulls them a bit and makes me less confident in them.
Do you feel like your worrying is causing you a lot of distress or discomfort?

Yes, it does cause me discomfort, I’d say. Not in a dramatic way all the time, but it’s there — this sort of constant unsettled feeling that makes ordinary things feel harder than they ought to be.

I still keep up with things, which is why part of me hesitates to say it’s “a lot,” because I’m not just staying at home doing nothing. I still go out into the garden, and I still go to book club, and I do try to keep involved. But I notice the difference in how I’m managing them. With book club, I’ll turn up less prepared than I’d like, and then I feel awkward about it because I used to be more organized. It’s not that anyone is scolding me, but I feel it myself.

And with the exhibition planning, I’ve definitely begun turning down parts of it that I probably would have taken on before. If something feels like it has too many details to keep track of, or too much responsibility, I find myself stepping back and letting someone else do it. That bothers me, because I don’t really want to be less involved. It just feels harder to manage than it used to.

So yes, it’s distressing in that way — not unbearable, but uncomfortable and discouraging, because I can see myself shrinking back from things a bit.
Has your worrying significantly impacted your ability to perform your daily tasks or maintain your relationships with others?

Yes… I think it has, though I wouldn’t want to overstate it and say I can’t function, because that wouldn’t be true. I do still keep up with my usual things. I’m still in the garden, and I still go to book club, and I see people there, so I haven’t really cut myself off.

But the way I do those things has changed a bit. With book club, for example, I’m still turning up, but I’m often not as prepared as I used to be. I’ll have meant to finish the reading properly, or to think about what I wanted to say, and then somehow I’ve spent the time feeling preoccupied or going over other bits and pieces in my head. Then I get there and feel a bit embarrassed, because I’m not contributing in quite the same way.

And with the exhibition planning, that’s where I notice it most in terms of daily tasks or responsibilities. I’ve started turning down parts of it that I probably would have taken on before. If something feels like it has too many details or too much organizing involved, I find myself saying, “Maybe someone else should do that,” even when part of me would like to help. It just feels harder to manage than it used to.

So I don’t think it’s ruining my relationships, exactly. I’m still showing up. But I’m less prepared, less willing to take things on, and probably a bit less present than I used to be.

Or I’ll get up and straighten a cushion, or move something on the table, or check that something is put away properly—not because it desperately needs doing, but because sitting still feels uncomfortable. It’s as if my body is looking for something to do while my mind is going over everything.

Sometimes I’ll think, “Why can’t you just sit quietly for five minutes?” But I feel too on edge, too keyed up. Even in a perfectly calm room, I don’t always feel calm inside.

No, I don’t think so. At least, not in the sense of having a particular ritual I feel I have to do, like checking something a certain number of times or repeating a routine to make the worry go away.

I do have habits, I suppose — I might look over my calendar more than once, or think through what I’m meant to be doing the next day, but that feels more like trying to reassure myself or get organized than a set ritual. I don’t feel like, “If I don’t do this exact thing, something terrible will happen.” It’s more just that my mind keeps circling around things, and I’ll try to settle it by going over them again.

So no, I haven’t noticed any specific ritual or routine like that. It’s more the worrying itself than anything I’m compelled to do because of it.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's worrying is excessive and uncontrollable

target_item.name: Uncontrollable_Worry

patient.answer:
Not really, no. I mean, I can sometimes distract myself for a bit, or I can tell myself very firmly, “You’ve already made the list, you’ve checked the dates, you’ve done what you can,” but it doesn’t seem to switch off just because I’ve said that.

That’s really part of what brings me in, I suppose. Once the worry gets going, it sort of keeps running in the background, even when there isn’t anything more for me to do about it. I’ll know, logically, that I’ve handled the practical side of things, but my mind keeps going back over it anyway — did I miss something, should I check again, what if I’ve forgotten some small detail.

So I wouldn’t say I’m able to control it most of the time. I can sometimes contain it, maybe, or keep functioning around it, but I don’t feel like I can reliably make it stop when I want to.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think so. Even when I’m not worrying about one particular thing, I often feel sort of wound up, like my body hasn’t got the message that there’s nothing urgent happening.

It happens at home quite a bit, which feels silly to say because I’m just in my own living room, where I should be comfortable. It’s not dramatic, exactly. I’m not pacing around all day. But quiet sitting doesn’t feel as restful as it used to. There’s this jumpy feeling, like I’m waiting for something, even if I couldn’t tell you what.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of obsessive thoughts

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I’d describe it that way, no. I mean, I do have thoughts I don’t particularly want — worries that pop up when I’d rather be thinking about something else — but they usually feel like ordinary worries that have got stuck on repeat, not like strange or shocking thoughts that come out of nowhere.

When you say “intrusive,” I think of something that feels very alien or disturbing, and I don’t really have that. It’s more that I’ll find myself thinking, “What if I’ve overlooked something?” or “What if this turns out badly?” and then I try not to dwell on it, but trying not to think about it doesn’t always work. It’s not so much that I’m suppressing some awful image or idea; it’s more like I’m trying to put the worry aside and my mind keeps picking it back up.

So… no, not in the way I think you mean. I have unwanted worries, certainly, but I wouldn’t say I have intrusive thoughts that I’m trying to suppress or ignore in a more specific sense.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of excessive anxiety about everyday things
doctor.question: Do you often worry about everyday things, like finances, health, or relationships, even when there's no apparent reason to worry?

target_item.name: Excessive_Anxiety_Worry
target_item.manifestation: My mind keeps roaming from the exhibition schedule to my daughter's travel plans to whether the house gutters need fixing, and small things start to feel as if they could unravel into something much bigger.

patient.answer:
Yes, I do. More than I think is reasonable, honestly. It isn’t always one big obvious problem — it’s more that my mind sort of wanders from one ordinary thing to the next and treats each one as if it might become serious if I don’t keep thinking about it.

For example, I’ll start thinking about the exhibition schedule — whether I’ve remembered the dates properly, whether something might clash, whether I’ve misunderstood some small arrangement — and then before I’ve even settled that, my mind has moved on to my daughter’s travel plans. I’ll wonder if she’s left enough time, if the trains or flights will be all right, whether I should check in with her, even when there’s no real reason to think anything is wrong.

And then it can shift again to the house, like the gutters. I’ll notice a bit of rain or remember they haven’t been looked at in a while, and suddenly it feels as though if I don’t think it through properly, it could turn into some much bigger problem — water damage, repairs, expense, all of that. I know that sounds like making a mountain out of a molehill, and part of me does know that, but in the moment these small everyday things start to feel as if they could unravel. So yes, even without an obvious reason, I do find myself worrying about ordinary things quite a lot.
